I am genuinely shocked by the effusive praise that the app has received. I downloaded it expecting something that would, at a minimum, feel useful. Yet, the app simply created additional friction in what could have been a great consolidator. The challenge is high, replace an ecosystem of time management and organizational apps. So, this should at the very least be as good as those other experiences. Additionally, it brands itself as particularly useful for people with ADHD — which I had been clinically diagnosed with, so it should be perfect, right? Wrong. Consider these three examples as how I knew the app wasn’t for me and that ultimately made it feel more gimmicky than actually useful: 1. I have a daily commute during which I regularly lose service. This also happens to be a great time to mess around with my schedule. For me, understanding context dependent patterns of behavior has been a huge win for helping me work with my sometimes floaty attention. The problem is, even basic things — like moving a past event/item from a previous day to the present day — cannot be done without an active internet connection. 2. I work Monday-Friday and thought it would be useful to have a high level to do list. Things like making the bed, reading a few times a week, exercise, and time to level up outside of work. Editing this schedule is incredibly tedious and requires repeated back and forth with the AI agent or manual editing of the schedule. When I took a week off of work to travel, or for Christmas a few weeks later, I should have been able to tell the agent to remove my tasks for those days. In the case of the former it repeatedly failed leaving me to do it manually. In the case of the latter it removed events on the wrong two days after confirming the correct days. I needed to manually shift over the events. Is there a universe where this just works? Sure. But my experience was that I wasted more time checking its work. 3. Remember that Christmas example from before? Well it turns out that somewhere in the process of rescheduling the time off to the correct days I managed to remove all subsequent occurrences of all my events/tasks. That would make it the second time I had to re-enter my entire schedule. Why manually? Because the agent is slow, imprecise, and inconsistent. It’s just faster to do it myself and to make tweaks with the agent, accept it’s not actually intelligent enough to understand and therefore not intelligent enough to manage my schedule/tasks. Occasionally it was brilliant, but more often than not it was a hassle to use.   There are also subtle things like the way my tasks shift in importance and prominence throughout a day or week that make it feel less useful, especially because there’s a missed opportunity for 1) giving feedback about when you actually manage to finish things, 2) what you do and don’t finish, 3) meaningful capture and integration of your scheduling goals into your interactions with the agent, or 4) just finding ways to leverage research and other user experiences to give feedback or suggestions.  All in all, not a great user experience for me. It seems to be doing well with many others, but personally I found it was less efficient that just using my phone’s built in calendar and reminder system, which also works using “AI” voice controls.   I would recommend more traditional methods of managing time for people with ADHD and to try this as an experiment, coming in with low expectations and allowing yourself to be surprised. Then I realized - in the prerecorded videos - Roxanne and Rich deal with different workloads that are appropriate for neurotypical and neurodivergent people. A great example of this is their de cluttering videos. While Roxanne deals with an overwhelming closet / wash room, Rich is dealing with a larger room. I was feeling a lot less ashamed - they are dealing with the same amount of struggle but Roxanne is trying to balance something more manageable.    The messy mode videos are the ones that struck home with being the most relatable and had me feeling the most comfortable. Rather than individual steps or a short body doubling video, these are your long videos with some sections you can jump between. Seeing the mess helped me feel a lot less ashamed because it was what I was dealing with at the time. The step by step instructions were great. I still think that some of the timed videos are a little too fast for me - I work best without shorter timers. And the live body doubling gets a lot to get used to - because I feel like I have to respond or be on camera. But honestly - if you say nothing and keep it in the background it works really well.
